lessons.title: Intro to AI and Rational Agents

materials.videoTitle: [CS188 SP24] LEC01 - Intro to AI, Rational Agents

notes.summary: CS188 opens with the field's framing: AI as rational agents — perceive, decide, act — evaluated by expected utility. The Berkeley Spring 2024 lecture recordings (the newest public edition, on the department's official channel) structure the term around the agent progression: search agents, game agents, Markov agents, and learning agents. This is the modern survey course for everything happening in AI.
notes.focus: Formalize a familiar game (chess-lite) as state, actions, transition, goal. Restating the world as search space is the course's first skill.

lecture.title: CS 188 — LEC02: State spaces, uninformed search

materials.videoTitle: [CS188 SP24] LEC02 - Search: State Spaces, Uninformed Search

notes.summary: Systematic state-space exploration: BFS (shallowest), DFS (deepest, not optimal), uniform-cost (cheapest by g(n)), with the frontier mechanics, the explored set, and completeness/optimality guarantees. Your 6.006 BFS/DFS lectures are the direct prerequisite — CS188 adds the optimality lens.
notes.focus: For one weighted graph, run UCS by hand and note the pop order. The pattern 'cheap nodes pop first' is everything Dijkstra taught you, agent-ified.

materials.videoTitle: [CS188 SP24] LEC03 - Search: Informed Search, A*, Heuristics

notes.summary: A* = UCS + admissible heuristic: f(n) = g(n) + h(n), optimal when h never overestimates. Consistency for graph search, dominance relations comparing heuristics, and the craft of designing heuristics (relaxations). This single lecture's machinery runs game pathfinding, robot motion planning, and puzzle solvers worldwide.
notes.focus: Prove A* tree-search optimality with an admissible h, in writing. Then design TWO heuristics for the 8-puzzle and show which dominates.

notes.summary: When the path doesn't matter, only the goal: hill climbing, simulated annealing (accepting bad moves on a temperature schedule), genetic algorithms, and beam search. Local search scales to huge spaces (chip layout, timetabling) where systematic search dies. This is also your first metaheuristic vocabulary.
notes.focus: Implement hill climbing for 8-queens, then count restarts needed. The restart statistics teach more about local minima than any diagram.

materials.videoTitle: [CS188 SP24] LEC05 - Games: Trees, Minimax, Pruning

notes.summary: Games add an opponent: minimax computes each player's best move assuming optimal opposition. Alpha-beta pruning cuts the tree dramatically with zero risk of changing the answer. Depth-limited search with evaluation functions scales minimax to real games — the exact design of classical chess engines.
notes.focus: Hand-run alpha-beta on a 3-level game tree and mark pruned branches. Then shuffle child order and re-run — the pruning count change is the move-ordering lesson.

materials.videoTitle: [CS188 SP24] LEC06 - Games: Expectimax, Monte Carlo Tree Search

notes.summary: Chance enters the tree: expectimax averages over probabilistic outcomes instead of minimizing over adversaries. Monte Carlo Tree Search (the idea behind AlphaGo's rollout phase) samples instead of enumerating. The minimax-expectimax contrast also previews 6.036's probabilistic reasoning.
notes.focus: Solve one expectimax tree by hand, then change one chance node's probabilities and re-solve. Watching the optimal move flip IS probabilistic planning.

notes.summary: The mathematical heart of AI decision-making: MDPs formalize sequential decisions under uncertainty with states, actions, transitions, rewards, and discounting. The Bellman equation defines optimal value recursively. Every RL headline you've read is an MDP plus a learning rule — this lecture is the foundation.
notes.focus: Write the Bellman equation for a 2-state MDP and solve it exactly. The linear system is small — solve it and you've solved RL's core object.

lessons.title: Value Iteration, Policy Iteration, and Reinforcement Learning

notes.summary: Solving MDPs: value iteration (repeated Bellman backup to fixed point) and policy iteration (evaluate, improve, repeat). Then model-free RL: Q-learning's update when the model is unknown, exploration vs exploitation, and the difference between on- and off-policy. This unit is the engine room of modern RL.
notes.focus: Run 3 sweeps of value iteration on a tiny gridworld by hand and watch V converge. Then write the Q-update for one transition — RL in one line.

notes.summary: Structured probability: Bayes nets encode joint distributions compactly via DAGs where each node's distribution depends only on its parents. D-separation reads conditional independencies off the graph. Your Stat 110 conditioning returns as a GRAPH you can reason over — the representation behind real diagnostic and language systems.
notes.focus: For a 3-node network, compute a full joint by hand, then answer two conditional queries by marginalizing. Enumeration is exponential — you'll WANT the efficient algorithms next.

notes.summary: Efficient inference: variable elimination factors (your 6.046J join intuition, probabilistically), forward-backward for HMMs over time, and particle filtering for tracking. Rejection, likelihood weighting, and Gibbs sampling approximate when exact inference is intractable — the toolset every real probabilistic system uses.
notes.focus: Run variable elimination on a small network, tracking factor sizes. The elimination ORDER's effect on cost is the lecture's one deep lesson.

materials.videoTitle: [CS188 SP24] LEC07 - Logic: Propositional Logic and Planning

notes.summary: Knowledge-based agents: propositional logic as a formal language (syntax, semantics, entailment), inference rules, and SAT-solving as search over assignments. Situation calculus and planning tie logic back to the agent story — deciding what to DO from what you KNOW. Your 18.404J theory and 6.046J NP-completeness meet here: SAT is NP-complete AND the practical engine of planners.
notes.focus: Write a small KB (4 facts, 2 rules) and check entailment by truth table, then by resolution. Both agreeing is your first verified inference.

notes.summary: Checkpoint across the agent progression: search (uninformed, informed, adversarial, expectimax), MDPs, and RL. Berkeley's exam style is trace-and-derive: hand-run algorithms on small instances and prove small properties. Your 6.006 + Stat 110 training makes this exam very winnable.
notes.focus: Work two past exam problems per unit with a timer. The gap between 'can solve' and 'can solve in 12 minutes' is what this exam tests.

lessons.title: Final: Learning Agents and Course Synthesis

materials.videoTitle: [CS188 SP24] LEC16 - Utility Theory, Rationality, Decision Networks

notes.summary: The close: decision networks unifying probabilities with utilities (VPI quantifies information's worth), learning agents connecting to 6.036's models, and the synthesis — the whole course is one arc: from searching state spaces to learning value functions. The final artifact: your agent-progression map, each stage adding one capability.
notes.focus: Write the agent progression from memory (search -> games -> MDP -> RL -> inference -> decisions). Each arrow adds uncertainty or learning — that's AI's history in one line.
